content.p: On the evening of 27 December 2011, Russ Faria came home from a weekly game night with friends to the house he shared with his wife, Betsy, outside Troy, Missouri. He found her on the living room floor. She had been stabbed 55 times. Within days he was charged with her murder, and in 2013 a Lincoln County jury convicted him. In June 2015 a judge ordered a new trial, and on 6 November 2015 a judge sitting without a jury found him not guilty.

The question of who killed Betsy Faria has stayed in court ever since. The friend who was the last known person to see her alive, Pam Hupp, was the prosecution's key witness against Russ and had been named beneficiary of Betsy's life insurance days before the killing. She is now charged with first-degree murder in Betsy's death. She denies it, is presumed innocent of that charge, and has not been tried. She is already serving life without parole for a different killing, in 2016, to which she entered an Alford plea.

St. Louis Magazine's account of the day begins with Betsy's illness. She had been treated for breast cancer since 2010 and had learned in October 2011 that it had spread to her liver. On 27 December she was due for chemotherapy at a cancer centre in St. Peters. She had texted Hupp that she did not need a ride, but Hupp drove there anyway, sat through the session, went home to O'Fallon for a quick dinner, and returned to drive Betsy to Troy. When they reached the driveway, Hupp phoned Russ and put Betsy on the line; she sang out a "Merry Christmas and Happy New Year".

Tuesday was Russ's game night. He worked from home until 5 p.m. and joined friends at Mike Corbin's house at about 6. According to the magazine, they watched films, and Russ and two others left about 9 p.m. He says he bought food at an Arby's and ate it on the 24.6-mile drive back to Troy. On the 911 call he said, "My wife killed herself", an assumption the magazine says struck first responders as ludicrous. A fire captain and an EMS supervisor both concluded she had been dead for more than an hour.

The magazine reports that Hupp told detectives she had dropped Betsy off in Troy at about 7 p.m., though her phone records showed a call to Betsy at 7:27 p.m. while she was still in Troy. Her account of whether she went inside the house changed between interviews. She also told police that Betsy had been afraid of her husband, that he drank heavily, and that Betsy meant to raise a plan to move back to Lake Saint Louis, nearer her chemotherapy and friends, that evening, which Hupp said would anger him.

Investigators settled quickly on the husband. The magazine says police read his emotional swings on the 911 call and at the scene as suspicious, and that detectives told him he had failed a polygraph. They also noted a pair of his slippers with Betsy's blood on them in his closet. Prosecutors also drew on what Hupp had said about the marriage. Russ was charged with first-degree murder and armed criminal action on 4 January 2012. His trial took place in November 2013.

His alibi was substantial. Four acquaintances told detectives he was with them between about 6 and 9 p.m., and his cellphone also placed him at the game night more than 20 miles from the Farias' home, FOX 2 reported. A crime-lab report found Betsy's blood on the murder weapon and excluded Russ as the source of the DNA profiles on it. Prosecutors had narrowed the time of death to between 7:20 and 9:41 p.m. In her closing argument, Lincoln County prosecutor Leah Askey described the killing as "the ultimate role play" and suggested that the friends had held Russ's phone so that it would register in another town while he committed the murder. The alibi witnesses told FOX 2 they learned of that accusation only after the trial; defence attorney Joel Schwartz asked why, if the state believed it, they had not been charged.
The jury convicted. NBC News reported that Russ was sentenced to life plus 30 years.

The fact that would later reshape the case was the life insurance. On 23 December 2011, four days before the killing, Betsy changed the beneficiary of her $150,000 State Farm policy, which had named her husband, to Hupp, according to LegalClarity's account of the court record, with a library employee witnessing the signature. NBC News wrote that no other friend or family member knew of the change. In a statement to police, Hupp said that Betsy had asked her to give the daughters some money once they were older.

Hupp collected the money. LegalClarity reports that she set up a $100,000 trust for Betsy's two daughters before the 2013 trial, withdrew $99,700 of it by December 2013, and revoked the trust in July 2014. The daughters sued for the money and lost; the Circuit Court of St. Charles County found that Hupp's reply of "Okay" was not an enforceable promise, and the Missouri Court of Appeals affirmed on 16 May 2017.

Schwartz challenged the conviction. According to NBC News, a judge granted a new trial in June 2015, citing evidence the first jury had not heard that could have changed its verdict, including information about Hupp, whom the defence presented as a possible alternative suspect. Faria said he was released on 15 June 2015. Reports differ on how long he was imprisoned: NBC News first said more than two years, FOX 2 more than three, and a later NBC report four years.

The retrial, in November 2015, was heard without a jury by Judge Steven Ohmer; NBC News reported in 2016 that he was the same judge who had granted the new trial, though a 2019 NBC report described the retrial as before another judge. This time Schwartz was allowed to point to Hupp as the person with motive and opportunity. Neither side called her. A detective testified that Hupp had told police for the first time that summer that she and Betsy had been lovers. Evidence at the retrial included the slippers and a note found on a laptop, purportedly Betsy's, saying she was "afraid" of her husband; the defence argued both could have been planted to frame him. The four alibi witnesses testified again.

Ohmer found Russ Faria not guilty and called the investigation "disturbing", NBC News reported. In July 2016 Faria sued the prosecutor and investigators, alleging fabricated evidence and a failure to investigate the other obvious suspect. Askey told the St. Louis Post-Dispatch that she stood behind the investigation. According to LegalClarity, the suit was settled in March 2020 for $2,050,000, paid by the county's insurer, with no admission of fault; Oxygen put the figure at $2 million.

In August 2016 the story took a turn that put Hupp back in the news. On 16 August she called 911 at 12:08 p.m. to say that a man was breaking into her O'Fallon home and that she had shot him. The man, 33-year-old Louis Gumpenberger, died at the scene. NBC News reported that he was identified by fingerprints and that police found $900 and a note in his pocket which, according to the probable cause statement, appeared to be instructions to kidnap Hupp, take "Russ's money" from her bank and kill her to collect the rest of $10,000. The name Faria was on it.

St. Charles County prosecutor Tim Lohmar said his theory was that Hupp had built a plan to make it look as if Russ had hired a hitman. He said investigators had found a 911 call from six days earlier, from a woman who said a driver of a dark SUV had claimed to be a Dateline producer and offered her $1,000 for a recorded sound bite; surveillance video matched the plate to an SUV owned by Hupp, and the woman picked Hupp out of a lineup. Dateline said it had not offered to pay anyone for sound bites and was not producing a story about 911 calls. Prosecutors charged Hupp with murder and armed criminal action, and she was held on a $2 million cash-only bond. Within about an hour of being taken into custody, she stabbed herself in the neck and wrists with a pen.

On 19 June 2019 Hupp entered an Alford plea, which allowed her to avoid a death-penalty trial without admitting guilt: she acknowledged that prosecutors had enough evidence to convict. She received life without parole. Her plea in that case is not a finding about Betsy's death.
content.h2: Charges against Hupp for Betsy's death
content.p: Newly elected Lincoln County prosecutor Mike Wood, who had campaigned on reopening the case, told Dateline in June 2019 that he would pull the file out and look at it again. On 12 July 2021 he announced a charge of first-degree murder and armed criminal action against Hupp. He said at the time that he would seek the death penalty, as Rolling Stone reported. At the news conference he said Hupp was the last person to see Betsy alive, that her phone records put her at or near the house when Betsy died, and that she lied about her whereabouts and details. Hupp pleaded not guilty.

The same day Wood announced an investigation into police and prosecutorial misconduct in the original case. He called the first investigation "one of the poorest examples of investigative work" that he or his team had ever encountered, and, according to Rolling Stone, cited the lack of blood on Russ, his alibi witnesses and phone data that put him far from the scene. Askey has denied wrongdoing.

Hupp's trial has moved more than once. The case was first sent to Greene County, in Springfield, about 200 miles from Lincoln County, after the defence asked for a change of venue. In October 2023 Wood dismissed and refiled the charges so as to seek a venue closer to home, saying travel was too much to ask of witnesses and Betsy's loved ones. A trial date of 3 August 2026 was set. At an April 2026 hearing, according to FOX 2, a new judge, Joseph Rathert of Jefferson County, delayed the trial until the following year; Hupp, who attended in person, told the judge she agreed to the delay. Wood said the new date could be much sooner than the 2028 date set by the prior judge.

The misconduct inquiry has led to charges against a former sheriff's deputy. On 3 June 2025 Michael Merkel, a crime scene investigator in the original case, was charged with two counts of perjury over his testimony in the 2013 trial, NBC News and LegalClarity reported. Prosecutors say he falsely testified that photographs of a Bluestar blood-detection test showed "absolutely nothing" because the camera had failed; they say the camera captured 132 images with complete metadata. Merkel's lawyer, Joel Eisenstein, called the charges a "political stunt" and said Merkel would be exonerated. Merkel had earlier been charged with stalking and harassing the detective who led the internal investigation and has pleaded not guilty to that. Wood said more charges could follow. LegalClarity reports that his perjury trial is set for September 2027.

No conviction for Betsy Faria's murder stands. Hupp remains imprisoned in Missouri for Gumpenberger's death. Her mother's 2013 death, which the St. Louis County medical examiner changed from "accidental" to "undetermined" in 2017, has produced no charges.
